```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(formex)
o <- fx_ontology()

## Pull a recipe column straight from the ontology, so the "format observed" and
## "stabilizer" columns in the tables below are exactly what the engine runs.
of <- function(type, fl = NULL, col) {
  r <- o[o$semantic_type == type, , drop = FALSE]
  if (!is.null(fl)) r <- r[r$format_label == fl, , drop = FALSE]
  r[[col]][1]
}
stab <- function(x, type, fl = NULL)
  paste(suppressWarnings(fx_stabilize(x, type, fl, warn = FALSE)$stable),
        collapse = " ;; ")
code <- function(s) paste0("<code>", s, "</code>")

## Build one RAW -> STABLE workflow row. Everything but `target` is live.
wrow <- function(raw, type, fl = NULL, target) {
  data.frame(
    RAW               = paste(raw, collapse = " ;; "),
    `semantic type`   = if (is.null(fl)) type else paste0(type, " / ", fl),
    `format observed` = code(of(type, fl, "data_format")),
    stabilizer        = code(of(type, fl, "raw_to_stable_transform")),
    `target format`   = target,
    STABLE            = stab(raw, type, fl),
    check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
wtable <- function(...) knitr::kable(rbind(...), row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE)
```

`guess_data_type()` tells you *what* a column is. **Stabilizing** is the other
half of `formex`: taking the raw values and rewriting them into a clean, standard,
analysis-ready form --- and attaching the rule that lets anyone reopen the file
without corrupting it. This is the package's workhorse data-management
functionality, and it is entirely **rule-driven**: every semantic type in the
ontology ships with a pre-set transformation recipe, so cleaning a column is a
lookup, not a bespoke script.

This guide explains the stabilizer by example, through a table that recurs
throughout:

| column | what it is |
|---|---|
| **RAW** | an example value as it arrives in the file |
| **semantic type** | where `guess_data_type()` placed it |
| **format observed** | the pattern the raw value matches, in `formex` syntax |
| **stabilizer** | the function the recipe runs |
| **target format** | what the cleaned value looks like |
| **STABLE** | the new, standardized value |

The one syntax rule: anything inside `{{ … }}` is parsed by `formex`; anything
outside is a human comment. (The full grammar is the *Formex: the
format-expression syntax* article.) Every "format observed" and "stabilizer"
cell below is read live from `fx_ontology()`, and every **STABLE** value is the
live output of `fx_stabilize()`.

## The workflow at a glance

```{r master, echo = FALSE}
wtable(
  wrow(c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020"),       "calendar",            target = "ISO 8601 date"),
  wrow(c("$2,300.00", "17,298$", "$-45"),    "usd",                 target = "numeric (unit: USD)"),
  wrow(c("California", "TX", "Ohio"),         "geographic", "us_state", target = "USPS 2-letter"),
  wrow(c("yes", "0", "t", "x", "no"),        "mixed",               target = "TRUE / FALSE"),
  wrow("40° 44' 55\" N, 74° 00' 22\" W", "lat_lon", "dms", target = "decimal degrees")
)
```

Read any row left to right: a messy RAW value, matched by a **format**, run
through a **stabilizer**, lands on a clean **STABLE** value. The rest of this
guide takes the main transformation families one at a time.

## Calendar dates: many ways in, one way out

Dates are the canonical case. The same day arrives written a dozen ways; the
stabilizer normalizes every one to unambiguous ISO `YYYY-MM-DD`, so the column is
internally consistent and no locale can re-read `03/04` as the wrong day.

```{r dates-table, echo = FALSE}
wtable(
  wrow(c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020"),       "calendar", target = "ISO 8601"),
  wrow(c("2019-03-15", "2020-12-31"),        "calendar", target = "ISO 8601"),
  wrow(c("March 15, 2019", "December 31, 2020"), "calendar", target = "ISO 8601")
)
```

```{r dates-run}
fx_stabilize(c("03/15/2019", "March 15, 2019", "2019-03-15"), "calendar")$stable
```

The recipe also hands back an **import rule** --- for a date, `{{ as_yyyymmdd }}`
--- that tells the next reader to load the clean value back as a true date, not
as text. Classification and stabilization speak the same ontology, so the output
of one flows straight into the other:

```{r dates-loop}
x     <- c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020", "01/01/2021")
route <- guess_data_type(x)$route
fx_stabilize(x, route$semantic_type)$stable
```

## Date-times and time zones: the zone is a *unit*

A timestamp is a date plus a clock. The stabilizer normalizes the *written form*
to ISO 8601 (`2019-03-15T14:30:00`), whatever shape it arrived in:

```{r dt-table, echo = FALSE}
wtable(
  wrow(c("2019-03-15 14:30:00", "2020-12-31 08:05:00"), "timestamp", target = "ISO 8601 date-time"),
  wrow(c("3/15/2019 14:30", "12/31/2020 8:05"),          "timestamp", target = "ISO 8601 date-time")
)
```

```{r dt-run}
fx_stabilize(c("2019-03-15 14:30:00", "3/15/2019 14:30"), "timestamp")$stable
```

**Where does the time zone go?** This is exactly what `unit_type` is for. The
`timestamp` leaf records its unit as `datetime; timezone`:

```{r dt-unit}
o$unit_type[o$semantic_type == "timestamp"]
```

Normalizing the *format* (how the clock is written) and converting the *unit*
(which zone it is in) are two different operations. `formex` always normalizes the
format; a zone *conversion* --- say, rendering a UTC column in US/Eastern --- is a
**unit conversion**, the same category of operation as Celsius→Fahrenheit or
calendar-year→fiscal-year. Those run through the transform planner
([`fx_plan_transform()`](../reference/fx_plan_transform.html)) and fire only when
a converter for that unit pair is registered. So the zone is never silently
dropped from the model: it is tracked as the unit, ready for a conversion step
when one is wired in.

## Geographic transformations

Geographies are a closed, table-backed vocabulary, which makes them ideal for
rule-driven cleaning: a `lookup` collapses every spelling to one canonical code,
and a coordinate recipe reprojects messy degree notations to decimal degrees.

```{r geo-table, echo = FALSE}
wtable(
  wrow(c("California", "TX", "Ohio"),  "geographic", "us_state",    target = "USPS 2-letter"),
  wrow(c("France", "FR"),              "geographic", "iso_country", target = "ISO 3166 alpha-2"),
  wrow(c("06037", "36061"),            "geographic", "county_fips", target = "5-digit FIPS"),
  wrow("40° 44' 55\" N, 74° 00' 22\" W", "lat_lon", "dms", target = "decimal degrees (EPSG:4326)")
)
```

```{r geo-run}
# free-text state names and abbreviations collapse to one canonical code
fx_stabilize(c("California", "TX", "Ohio", "new york"), "geographic", "us_state")$stable

# a degrees-minutes-seconds pair is reprojected to decimal degrees, latitude first
fx_stabilize("40° 44' 55\" N, 74° 00' 22\" W", "lat_lon", "dms")$stable
```

Note the `county_fips` import rule is `{{ as_factor }}`, and the broader
`geographic` *key* type hardens a numeric GEOID by prefixing it (`FIPS-06037`) so
no spreadsheet can strip its leading zero. The recipe is selective, too: a value
that is not a valid 5-digit county (a stray 4-digit form number, say) stabilizes
to `NA` rather than being force-padded into a bogus code.

## Cleaning messy variables

The same machinery tidies the everyday mess of real survey and administrative
data.

**Currencies** strip symbols and grouping marks and return a bare number you can
compute on --- while the currency itself rides along as the `unit_type` rather
than being buried in the text. European notation (dot-thousands, comma-decimal)
is a separate leaf with its own recipe:

```{r clean-currency, echo = FALSE}
wtable(
  wrow(c("$2,300.00", "17,298$", "$-45"), "usd",  target = "numeric (unit: USD)"),
  wrow(c("2.300,00 €", "€ 45,00"), "euro", target = "numeric (unit: EUR)")
)
```

**Mixed-encoding booleans** --- the classic IRS-990 case where one column holds
`yes`, `0`, `t`, and a bare `x` --- collapse to clean logicals:

```{r clean-bool, echo = FALSE}
wtable(
  wrow(c("yes", "0", "t", "x", "no"), "mixed", target = "TRUE / FALSE")
)
```

```{r clean-bool-run}
fx_stabilize(c("yes", "0", "t", "x", "no"), "mixed")$stable
```

**Ordered categories** keep their level order for analysis. The code→label
dictionary lives alongside the data; the recipe records that the result is an
ordered factor:

```{r clean-ordered, echo = FALSE}
wtable(
  wrow(c("1", "2", "3", "2", "1"), "ordered", target = "ordered factor")
)
```

In every case the stabilizer reports what it could *not* convert rather than
failing silently --- the `conversion_log` in the `fx_stabilize()` return records
how many present values were dropped to `NA`, and why.

## Bring your own: a custom stabilizer

The shipped recipes cover the common cases, but a project often needs its own ---
collapsing a column into house-specific buckets, applying an internal coding
scheme. The design is open: a stabilizer is just an R function of the values, and
a recipe names it in its **stabilizer** column. You keep your project's functions
in a small script --- call it `dg.R` --- and the recipe refers to them by name.

Say you want to collapse US states into Census regions. The function, as it would
live in `dg.R`:

```{r custom-fn}
# --- dg.R : project-specific stabilizers ------------------------------------
as_region <- function(x, a = NA) {
  region <- c(
    CT = "Northeast", ME = "Northeast", MA = "Northeast", NH = "Northeast",
    RI = "Northeast", VT = "Northeast", NJ = "Northeast", NY = "Northeast",
    PA = "Northeast",
    IL = "Midwest", IN = "Midwest", MI = "Midwest", OH = "Midwest",
    WI = "Midwest", IA = "Midwest", KS = "Midwest", MN = "Midwest",
    MO = "Midwest", NE = "Midwest", ND = "Midwest", SD = "Midwest",
    DE = "South", FL = "South", GA = "South", MD = "South", NC = "South",
    SC = "South", VA = "South", DC = "South", WV = "South", AL = "South",
    KY = "South", MS = "South", TN = "South", AR = "South", LA = "South",
    OK = "South", TX = "South",
    AZ = "West", CO = "West", ID = "West", MT = "West", NV = "West",
    NM = "West", UT = "West", WY = "West", AK = "West", CA = "West",
    HI = "West", OR = "West", WA = "West")
  unname(region[toupper(trimws(x))])
}
```

Once that name is registered in `formex`'s verb library (assume it is wired in
here), an ontology row can reference it in its **stabilizer** column exactly like
a built-in, and the workflow table reads the same as every row above:

```{r custom-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  RAW               = "NY ;; CA ;; TX ;; IL",
  `semantic type`   = "geographic / us_region",
  `format observed` = code("{{ lexicon:usps_state }}"),
  stabilizer        = code("{{ as_region }}"),
  `target format`   = "census_region (factor)",
  STABLE            = paste(as_region(c("NY", "CA", "TX", "IL")), collapse = " ;; "),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE)
```

```{r custom-run}
# the recipe's stabilizer, applied directly
as_region(c("NY", "CA", "TX", "IL"))
```

That is the whole point of a rule-driven engine: whether a transformation ships
with the package or you wrote it this morning, it plugs into the same
RAW → format → stabilizer → STABLE pathway, and the resulting file is cleaned and
self-describing by the same rules.
